patient.name: Tomasz Kowalski
patient.complaint: Fever, strange behaviour and a first seizure after a flu-like illness
background: No regular medicines, no known drug allergies
Bus driver, lives with his partner in Ealing

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with fever plus confusion, behaviour change, seizures or focal signs, often without meningism. A young woman with psychosis, seizures and an ovarian mass is anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

points: Tomasz, 34: four days of a **flu-like illness**.
Today his partner found him muddled, saying odd things.
He complained of a **burning smell** nobody else noticed.
In the ambulance: a **generalised seizure**, his first ever.

steps.lead: Tomasz's fever with **altered mental state** points to the brain tissue itself, not just the meninges.

points: Disorientated in time and place; word-finding difficulty.
Reflexes **brisk** on the right; plantars equivocal.

steps.lead: Fever, confusion, a new seizure and **focal neurology** after a flu-like illness: Tomasz has the acute viral encephalitis picture.

steps.q: Tomasz has fever, confusion, a seizure and smell hallucinations. Which cause is most likely?
steps.r: **HSV-1** is the commonest cause of viral encephalitis and loves the **temporal lobes**, which explains the smell hallucinations.

steps.lead: Tomasz fits **HSV**: temporal lobe features (smell, speech, seizure). A young woman with psychosis and an ovarian teratoma would suggest anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

steps.text: **Olfactory hallucinations**, odd behaviour and temporal seizures plus fever = HSV encephalitis until proven otherwise. Treat first, confirm later.

steps.lead: Tomasz has no recent vaccination and a single focus. **ADEM** would give multifocal demyelination weeks after an infection or vaccine.

steps.title: Which encephalitis?
nodes: Temporal features, cold sores → HSV encephalitis
Young woman, psychosis, ovarian mass → anti-NMDA
Weeks after infection or vaccine, multifocal → ADEM
steps.caption: The extra feature names the type.

steps.text: Do not call confusion with fever and no neck stiffness 'just delirium'. **Absent meningism** is typical of encephalitis; focal signs or a new seizure demand an LP.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (CSF HSV PCR, or anti-NMDA receptor antibodies for autoimmune) and 'Which is the most likely CSF finding?' (lymphocytes, raised protein, normal glucose).

points: CT head first: GCS 12 and a seizure; no mass effect.

visual.title: Tomasz's GCS on arrival
visual.label: Tomasz 12
visual.caption: Reduced consciousness plus a seizure: CT before LP to exclude raised pressure.

steps.lead: After a full neurological exam, Tomasz's **LP** is the first-line test. His CSF should show a viral pattern.

steps.title: Tomasz's CSF
steps.text: Lymphocytes, raised protein, normal glucose: viral. Red cells hint at HSV's haemorrhagic necrosis.

visual.title: CSF glucose : serum ratio
visual.label: Tomasz 0.65
visual.caption: A normal glucose ratio fits viral encephalitis; bacteria consume glucose.

steps.q: Which test on Tomasz's CSF confirms the diagnosis?
steps.r: **CSF viral PCR**, particularly HSV PCR, is the gold standard for viral encephalitis. Oligoclonal bands suggest MS.

steps.lead: Tomasz's **CSF HSV-1 PCR** comes back positive. If it were negative with psychosis and seizures, anti-NMDA antibodies would be sent.
Tomasz's MRI shows **temporal lobe** high signal, typical of HSV encephalitis.

steps.text: A normal CT does not exclude encephalitis. CT is a safety check before LP; **MRI** shows the temporal lobes and **PCR** confirms the virus.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': IV aciclovir immediately without waiting for results, IV ceftriaxone too if meningitis is possible (plus amoxicillin over 60), and steroids plus IVIg for autoimmune encephalitis.

steps.q: Tomasz is febrile and confused with a new seizure. When should aciclovir start?
steps.r: **Do not wait.** Untreated HSV encephalitis carries high mortality, so IV aciclovir starts on suspicion.

steps.lead: Tomasz could still have meningitis, so he gets **IV ceftriaxone** plus **high-dose IV aciclovir** at once. At 34 he does not need amoxicillin.

visual.title: Age and Listeria cover
visual.label: Tomasz 34
visual.caption: Over 60, add IV amoxicillin to cover Listeria.

steps.title: Suspected encephalitis: first hour
nodes: Fever + altered mental state or seizure
IV aciclovir now (± ceftriaxone, ± amoxicillin if >60)
CT if GCS low or focal signs, then LP

steps.lead: Tomasz gets **levetiracetam** for seizures and close neuro observation; a falling GCS would mean **ICU**.

visual.title: Tomasz on IV aciclovir
visual.caption: A 14 to 21 day IV course; recovery can leave memory problems.

steps.lead: Had Tomasz's PCR been negative and anti-NMDA antibodies positive, he would need **IV methylprednisolone and IVIg**, then rituximab if no response.
UK guidance: start **aciclovir** on suspicion and co-treat for meningitis until bacteria are excluded, exactly Tomasz's plan.

steps.text: **Dexamethasone** is for bacterial (pneumococcal) meningitis, not HSV encephalitis. Steroids belong in **autoimmune** encephalitis.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why HSV targets the temporal lobes, the antibody target in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, or the mechanism of ADEM.

steps.lead: Tomasz's cold sore virus reactivated and tracked back along the **olfactory/trigeminal** nerves: hence the burning smell and the red cells in his CSF.

steps.title: From cold sore to temporal lobe
nodes: HSV-1 latent in the trigeminal ganglion

steps.q: Why does Tomasz's CSF contain red cells?
o: Haemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobe
steps.r: HSV causes **haemorrhagic necrosis**, so red cells can appear in the CSF.

steps.lead: Unlike Tomasz, anti-NMDA patients have **antibodies to the NR1 subunit**, often triggered by an **ovarian teratoma** containing neural tissue.
ADEM is the immune system's mistake after an infection or vaccine: **molecular mimicry** against myelin, not active infection like Tomasz's.

steps.text: Haemorrhagic necrosis is why every hour counts: the brain damage of HSV encephalitis is fast, so **aciclovir starts before PCR returns**.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of viral encephalitis?
Which tumour is linked to anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis?
mcq.r: **Ovarian teratoma** in young women; it contains neural tissue that triggers the antibodies.

mcq.q: Which feature best separates encephalitis from meningitis?
o: Altered mental state and focal neurology
mcq.r: Encephalitis affects brain tissue: **confusion, seizures and focal signs**, often without meningism.

o: Demyelination after a viral illness or vaccination

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard test for viral encephalitis?
mcq.r: **CSF PCR** (particularly HSV PCR) confirms the virus.

mcq.q: What does the CSF show in viral encephalitis?
Which MRI finding is typical of HSV encephalitis?
When is IV aciclovir started in suspected encephalitis?
mcq.r: **Do not wait**: untreated HSV encephalitis has high mortality.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for autoimmune encephalitis?
mcq.r: **IV methylprednisolone and IVIg**, plus tumour removal; rituximab/cyclophosphamide if no response in 2 weeks.

mcq.q: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis antibodies target which subunit?

technique.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 3 day history of fever and headache. Today her husband says she is behaving strangely and she complained of a smell of burning rubber. She then has a generalised seizure. She has a history of cold sores. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. She is confused, with mild neck stiffness and no rash.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis with fever and neurological change: is it the meninges or the brain itself?
Behaviour change, **olfactory hallucination** (temporal lobe), a seizure, confusion, minimal meningism and HSV history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fever + altered mental state + temporal features = **HSV encephalitis**.

elim: Bacterial meningitis gives marked meningism; altered behaviour and smell hallucinations point to the brain itself.
An abscess is usually subacute with a known source and focal signs.
SAH is a sudden thunderclap headache, not a 3 day febrile illness.
Viral meningitis does not cause confusion, seizures or hallucinations.

steps.x: **C. Herpes simplex encephalitis.** Rule: fever + confusion/seizure + temporal features = HSV; start aciclovir now.

technique.stem: A 29 year old man has fever, confusion and a new seizure. He is started on IV aciclovir. A CT head is normal. A lumbar puncture shows a white cell count of 150 /mm³ (95% lymphocytes), protein 0.8 g/L and CSF:serum glucose ratio 0.7.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: 'Confirm the diagnosis': the gold-standard test.

clues: fever, confusion and a new seizure
steps.x: Viral CSF pattern in a patient with encephalitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Viral encephalitis is confirmed with **CSF viral PCR**, particularly HSV PCR.

elim: Blood cultures look for bacteraemia; the CSF is viral.
Contrast CT adds little; MRI is the imaging of choice.
EEG may show temporal changes but does not confirm the cause.
Serum HSV antibodies only show past exposure.

steps.x: **B. CSF HSV PCR.** Rule: viral encephalitis = CSF PCR; autoimmune = antibody testing.

technique.stem: A 36 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department with a 2 day history of fever, headache and increasing confusion. She had a seizure on arrival. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. A CT head is normal. A lumbar puncture has been sent and results are awaited.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: Next step, with results still pending.
Suspected encephalitis; nothing is confirmed yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Start **high-dose IV aciclovir** now: do not wait.

elim: Waiting risks death; untreated HSV encephalitis has high mortality.
Dexamethasone is for bacterial meningitis.
Methylprednisolone is for autoimmune encephalitis.
Oral antivirals are not adequate for encephalitis.

steps.x: **B. IV aciclovir.** Rule: suspect encephalitis = IV aciclovir before results.

technique.stem: A 23 year old woman has a 2 week history of anxiety, paranoid delusions and hallucinations, followed by seizures and abnormal mouth movements. A pelvic MRI shows a left ovarian teratoma. CSF shows a mild lymphocytosis and no pathogens are identified.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her illness?
o: Autoantibodies against the NR1 subunit of NMDA receptors
Direct viral invasion of the temporal lobe

steps.x: A mechanism question: name the condition, then its mechanism.
Young woman, psychosis then seizures, ovarian teratoma, no infection: **anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Paraneoplastic **autoantibodies against the NR1 subunit** of the NMDA receptor.

elim: AChR antibodies cause myasthenia gravis.
VGCC antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
Viral invasion is HSV; no pathogen was found.
Molecular mimicry against myelin is ADEM.

steps.x: **C. Autoantibodies against the NR1 subunit.** Rule: young woman + psychosis + teratoma = anti-NMDA.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has a 5 day history of a flu-like illness. Today he became confused and had a seizure. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He is disorientated with expressive dysphasia and brisk reflexes on the right. There is no neck stiffness or rash. Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, confusion, seizure and focal signs without meningism after a flu-like illness, with a viral CSF, is HSV encephalitis. Viral meningitis does not alter mental state.

steps.x: Diagnosis: meninges or brain parenchyma?
**Altered mental state**, seizure and focal neurology without meningism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Viral encephalitis, most commonly **HSV**.

elim: CSF has lymphocytes and normal glucose; no meningism.
No source, subacute course or ring lesion.
No thunderclap headache.
Viral meningitis spares mental state and does not cause focal signs.

steps.x: **C. Herpes simplex encephalitis.** Rule: confusion and focal signs with fever = encephalitis.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman is brought in by her flatmate. Over 10 days she has become anxious, then paranoid and is hearing voices. Today she had two seizures and has odd chewing movements. She had a cold 3 weeks ago. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 152/94 mmHg. A pelvic ultrasound shows a complex right ovarian mass.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A young woman with psychosis then seizures, dyskinesia, autonomic instability and an ovarian mass (teratoma) after a viral illness has anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a young woman with psychosis and seizures.
Psychosis plus seizures, dyskinesia, preceding viral illness and an **ovarian teratoma**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.**

elim: ADEM is multifocal demyelination, not psychosis with a teratoma.
No meningism or high fever.
Schizophrenia does not cause seizures or dyskinesia.
HSV gives fever and temporal features, no ovarian mass link.

steps.x: **B. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.** Rule: psychosis + seizures + ovarian teratoma.

practice.stem: An 8 year old boy has had chickenpox 2 weeks ago. Over 2 days he has become drowsy, unsteady and has weakness of his left leg and blurred vision. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. MRI brain and spine show multiple large, patchy white matter lesions of similar age.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Multifocal demyelination with encephalopathy weeks after a viral infection in a child is acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, thought to be molecular mimicry.

steps.x: Diagnosis: what is the timing relative to the infection?

clues: multiple large, patchy white matter lesions of similar age
steps.x: Post-infectious, encephalopathy, **multifocal demyelination**, all the same age (one event).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ADEM**.

elim: An abscess is a single ring-enhancing lesion.
GBS is peripheral: ascending weakness, areflexia, no brain lesions.
HSV targets the temporal lobes, not diffuse white matter.
MS lesions are of different ages and drowsiness is unusual.

steps.x: **A. ADEM.** Rule: weeks after infection or vaccine + multifocal demyelination + encephalopathy.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has fever, confusion and a seizure. MRI shows high signal in the left temporal lobe. CSF shows a lymphocytosis with red cells, raised protein and a normal glucose.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: HSV-1 is the most common cause of viral encephalitis and characteristically affects the temporal lobes with haemorrhagic necrosis (red cells in CSF).

steps.x: Causative organism of an encephalitis.
Encephalitis, temporal lobe, viral CSF with **haemorrhagic** features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Enterovirus usually causes viral meningitis.
Listeria affects over-60s and immunosuppressed, often rhombencephalitis.
Meningococcus causes meningitis with a rash and neutrophils.
VZV is less common and usually follows a rash.

steps.x: **B. HSV-1.** Rule: temporal lobe + red cells in CSF = HSV.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has a 6 week history of worsening short-term memory. His wife describes several daily episodes where he stares and 'zones out' for a minute. He has had no fever. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. MRI shows bilateral medial temporal lobe high signal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Subacute short-term memory loss with absence-like 'zoning out' seizures and medial temporal high signal is limbic encephalitis, an autoimmune encephalitis.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a subacute memory problem with episodes.

clues: bilateral medial temporal lobe high signal
steps.x: Subacute memory loss, absence-like seizures, limbic system inflamed on MRI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Limbic encephalitis.**

elim: Absence epilepsy starts in childhood and spares memory.
Alzheimer's evolves over years, not weeks, and has no seizures.
Delirium is acute and fluctuating with a trigger.
TGA is a single episode of amnesia lasting hours.

steps.x: **D. Limbic encephalitis.** Rule: weeks of memory loss + 'zoning out' seizures + medial temporal signal.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man had a painful vesicular rash over his right chest wall 10 days ago. For 2 days he has had fever, headache and increasing confusion. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg. He is disorientated with no neck stiffness. Urine dipstick is negative. Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Confusion and fever after shingles, with a lymphocytic CSF, is VZV encephalitis, one of the viral causes alongside HSV.

steps.x: Diagnosis: link the rash to the confusion.
Recent **shingles**, then encephalopathy; the CSF is lymphocytic and there is no other source.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **VZV encephalitis.**

elim: CSF is lymphocytic with no organisms.
Urine is clear and the CSF is abnormal.
Neuralgia is pain only, not fever or confusion.
Ramsay Hunt is VZV of the facial nerve: ear vesicles and facial palsy.

steps.x: **E. Varicella zoster encephalitis.** Rule: shingles + fever + confusion + lymphocytic CSF.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 2 week history of agitation, visual hallucinations and insomnia, then seizures. She had a viral illness a month ago. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 148/92 mmHg. Investigations:
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: CSF and serum anti-NMDA receptor antibodies
practice.e: Psychosis and seizures in a young woman with a mild lymphocytosis and negative PCR suggest autoimmune encephalitis, confirmed by CSF/serum anti-NMDA receptor antibodies. Pelvic imaging then looks for a teratoma.

steps.x: 'Diagnostic': which test confirms the suspected cause?
Psychiatric onset, then seizures; CSF shows mild lymphocytosis, negative HSV PCR and no pathogen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Autoimmune encephalitis is confirmed by **CSF/serum autoantibodies**.

elim: PCR is already negative and the picture is autoimmune.
CT is a safety scan, not diagnostic.
EEG shows abnormal activity but not the cause.
Ultrasound finds a teratoma but does not confirm encephalitis.

steps.x: **A. Anti-NMDA receptor antibodies.** Rule: viral = PCR; autoimmune = antibodies.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has fever, confusion and an olfactory hallucination. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. He has no neck stiffness. A CT head is normal and a lumbar puncture is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely CSF finding?
o: Normal cell count with very high protein
practice.e: Viral encephalitis gives a lymphocytosis, raised protein and normal glucose. Neutrophils with low glucose is bacterial meningitis.

steps.x: Expected CSF result: name the condition first.

clues: fever, confusion and an olfactory hallucination
steps.x: Temporal lobe encephalitis: probable **HSV**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Viral pattern: **lymphocytes, raised protein, normal glucose**.

elim: That is bacterial meningitis.
Albuminocytological dissociation is Guillain-Barré.
Oligoclonal bands alone suggest MS.
Xanthochromia is subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.x: **A. Lymphocytosis, raised protein, normal glucose.** Rule: viral CSF = lymphocytes + normal glucose.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has a 1 day history of fever, headache, neck stiffness and confusion. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 114 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. There is no rash. Encephalitis and meningitis are both suspected. Blood cultures have been taken.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: When encephalitis and meningitis overlap, treat both empirically with IV ceftriaxone and IV aciclovir, adding IV amoxicillin over 60 to cover Listeria.

steps.x: Initial empirical treatment; check the age.
Overlap picture in someone **over 60**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ceftriaxone + aciclovir + amoxicillin** (Listeria).

elim: Leaves bacterial meningitis untreated.
Leaves HSV untreated.
Misses Listeria cover in over-60s.
Oral treatment is never adequate here.

steps.x: **D. IV ceftriaxone, amoxicillin and aciclovir.** Rule: over 60 = add amoxicillin.

practice.stem: A 22 year old woman has psychosis, seizures and reduced consciousness. CSF and serum anti-NMDA receptor antibodies are positive and a pelvic MRI shows an ovarian teratoma. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 156/96 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV methylprednisolone and IVIg with teratoma removal
practice.e: First line for autoimmune encephalitis is IV methylprednisolone and IVIg, with removal of any teratoma. Rituximab and cyclophosphamide are second line.

steps.x: Initial management of a confirmed autoimmune encephalitis.
Confirmed anti-NMDA encephalitis with a tumour trigger.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV methylprednisolone + IVIg**, and remove the teratoma.

elim: Antipsychotics do not treat the cause and can worsen her.
Not viral.
Oral steroids are not adequate.
Second line, if no response in 2 weeks.

steps.x: **C. IV methylprednisolone and IVIg with teratoma removal.**

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis had her ovarian teratoma removed and completed IV methylprednisolone and IVIg. Two weeks later she remains agitated with ongoing seizures and no improvement. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 140/88 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: No response to first-line therapy within 2 weeks means second-line immunotherapy: rituximab and cyclophosphamide.

steps.x: 'Next step' after first-line has failed.
First line completed, no response at **2 weeks**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Second line: **rituximab and cyclophosphamide**.

elim: Treats symptoms only and risks harm.
Not a viral cause.
A step down, not escalation.
Ongoing seizures need escalation.

steps.x: **D. Rituximab and cyclophosphamide.** Rule: no response in 2 weeks = second line.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man with recurrent cold sores develops fever, confusion and olfactory hallucinations. MRI shows high signal in the medial temporal and inferior frontal lobes. CSF HSV-1 PCR is positive.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the distribution of brain involvement?
o: Antibodies against the NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor
Direct spread from the middle ear
Haematogenous spread across the choroid plexus
Reactivation with retrograde spread along trigeminal or olfactory nerves
practice.e: HSV-1 reactivates and spreads retrogradely along trigeminal/olfactory pathways to the temporal and frontal lobes, causing haemorrhagic necrosis.

steps.x: Why these lobes? A mechanism question.

clues: medial temporal and inferior frontal lobes
steps.x: Latent HSV, smell pathway, temporal-frontal distribution.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reactivation and retrograde neural spread** along trigeminal/olfactory pathways.

elim: That is anti-NMDA encephalitis.
Otogenic spread causes an abscess.
Haematogenous spread is bacterial meningitis.
That is ADEM.

steps.x: **E. Retrograde spread along trigeminal or olfactory nerves.**

prompts.q: What is encephalitis and how does it present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the brain tissue is involved, so mental state changes early.

points.p: Inflammation of the brain parenchyma, viral or autoimmune
Altered mental state, confusion, personality change

points.why: Confusion with no neck stiffness still needs an LP.

prompts.q: What is the commonest cause of viral encephalitis, and which lobes does it hit?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: smell hallucinations = temporal lobe.

points.why: VZV after shingles is a variant stem.

prompts.q: How do autoimmune, limbic encephalitis and ADEM present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the extra clue names the type.

points.p: Anti-NMDA: young women, psychosis, seizures, ovarian teratoma
Limbic: short-term memory loss, 'zoning out' seizures
ADEM: demyelination after viral illness or vaccination

prompts.q: Which features separate encephalitis from meningitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: decide meninges vs parenchyma before anything else.

points.p: Encephalitis: confusion, seizures and focal signs
Meningitis: prominent meningism, mental state often preserved early
points.why: Overlap exists: treat both if unsure.

prompts.q: What are the first-line and gold-standard investigations?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'diagnostic' means PCR or antibodies.

points.p: First line: full neurological exam then lumbar puncture
points.why: CT first if GCS low or focal signs.
Second line; CT may be normal.

prompts.q: What does the CSF show in viral encephalitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: compare with the bacterial pattern.

points.why: Low glucose suggests bacteria or TB.

prompts.q: What is the immediate treatment of suspected encephalitis, and why not wait?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'await results' is always the wrong answer.

points.p: Untreated HSV encephalitis has high mortality
Add IV ceftriaxone if meningitis is possible

prompts.q: How is autoimmune encephalitis treated, and what supportive care is needed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: steroids belong here, not in HSV.

points.p: No response in 2 weeks: rituximab and cyclophosphamide
Supportive: seizure control, ICU if needed
points.why: Airway at risk if GCS falls.

prompts.q: Why does HSV hit the temporal lobes, and what is the mechanism of anti-NMDA encephalitis and ADEM?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three mechanisms, three clues.

points.p: HSV: reactivation and retrograde spread along trigeminal/olfactory pathways
Anti-NMDA: autoantibodies against the NR1 subunit, from ovarian teratoma

points.why: Immune cross-reaction after infection or vaccine.

glossary.Encephalitis: Inflammation of the brain tissue itself, usually viral or autoimmune.
glossary.Parenchyma: The functional tissue of an organ; here, the brain substance rather than its coverings.
glossary.Meningism: Neck stiffness, photophobia and headache from irritated meninges.
glossary.Encephalopathy: Diffuse brain dysfunction causing confusion or reduced consciousness.
glossary.HSV: Herpes simplex virus; type 1 causes cold sores and most viral encephalitis.
glossary.HSV-1: Herpes simplex virus type 1, the commonest cause of viral encephalitis.
glossary.VZV: Varicella zoster virus, which causes chickenpox and shingles.
glossary.Olfactory hallucination: Smelling something that is not there, a sign of temporal lobe involvement.
glossary.Temporal lobe: The brain lobe for memory, smell and language; HSV's favourite target.
glossary.Limbic encephalitis: Autoimmune inflammation of the limbic system causing memory loss and seizures.
glossary.Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: Autoimmune encephalitis from antibodies to the NMDA receptor, often with an ovarian teratoma.
glossary.NMDA: A glutamate receptor in the brain, the target of anti-NMDA receptor antibodies.
glossary.NR1 subunit: The part of the NMDA receptor targeted by the autoantibodies.
glossary.Ovarian teratoma: A germ cell tumour of the ovary that can contain neural tissue.
glossary.Paraneoplastic: Caused by the immune response to a tumour rather than by the tumour itself.
glossary.ADEM: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis: demyelination after an infection or vaccination.
glossary.Molecular mimicry: When antibodies to a microbe cross-react with the body's own proteins.
glossary.Demyelination: Damage to the myelin sheath that insulates nerve fibres.
glossary.Lumbar puncture: A needle into the lower spine to sample cerebrospinal fluid.
glossary.CSF: Cerebrospinal fluid, which surrounds the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.PCR: Polymerase chain reaction, which detects viral genetic material.
glossary.Lymphocytosis: Raised lymphocyte count; in CSF, suggests a viral or autoimmune cause.
glossary.Xanthochromia: Yellow CSF from broken-down blood, typical of subarachnoid haemorrhage.
glossary.Haemorrhagic necrosis: Tissue death with bleeding; why HSV encephalitis can put red cells in the CSF.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale, scored 3 to 15; 8 or less means the airway is at risk.
glossary.Aciclovir: An antiviral given IV at high dose for HSV and VZV encephalitis.
glossary.Ceftriaxone: A third-generation cephalosporin used empirically for bacterial meningitis.
glossary.Listeria: A bacterium causing meningitis in over-60s, pregnancy and immunosuppression; needs amoxicillin.
glossary.IVIg: Intravenous immunoglobulin, pooled antibodies used to dampen autoimmune disease.
glossary.Methylprednisolone: A high-dose IV corticosteroid used in autoimmune encephalitis.
glossary.Plasma exchange: Removing the patient's plasma to clear harmful antibodies.
glossary.Rituximab: An anti-CD20 antibody that depletes B cells; second line in autoimmune encephalitis.
glossary.Cyclophosphamide: An immunosuppressive drug used as second line in autoimmune encephalitis.
glossary.Brisk reflexes: Exaggerated tendon reflexes, suggesting upper motor neurone or CNS involvement.
glossary.Expressive dysphasia: Difficulty producing speech despite knowing what to say.
glossary.Dyskinesia: Involuntary movements, such as chewing or writhing, seen in anti-NMDA encephalitis.
glossary.Levetiracetam: An anti-seizure medicine often used for seizures in acute brain illness.
